Of the many, many things we’re not supposed to snack on, perhaps the most common forbidden food is silica gel. This tiny packet pops up in packaging for everything — from TVs and guitar cases to sunscreen and snack foods. So why is silica gel everywhere, and what would actually happen if you ate it? Vivian Jiang digs into the science of this pervasive product.

snippet.title: Dogs Trained for War in WWII
snippet.description:
During World War II, armies around the world used many unexpected tools in warfare — including highly trained dogs.

The United States Marine Corps and other military units created specialized war dog training programs to prepare dogs for real combat missions. These animals were not just mascots or companions. They were trained soldiers with specific battlefield roles.

War dogs were taught to carry messages between units when radios failed or when communication lines were too dangerous. In dense jungles and chaotic battlefields, these dogs could move quickly and quietly, delivering critical information that sometimes meant the difference between life and death.

Some dogs were trained to carry ammunition and supplies directly to soldiers at the front lines. Others learned to detect hidden enemies or warn their handlers about approaching danger long before humans could notice anything.

Because of their senses — especially their hearing and smell — dogs were extremely valuable in environments where visibility was limited, such as jungles, forests, and nighttime operations.

Training often took place at military facilities like the Marine war dog training programs in North Carolina, where both dogs and their handlers learned to operate together under intense conditions. The bond between a war dog and its handler was essential. Trust and loyalty allowed them to function as a team in dangerous situations.

These dogs ran through gunfire, crossed rivers, navigated rough terrain, and carried out missions that would have been nearly impossible for humans alone.

They did not understand politics or strategy. They simply followed their training and their handlers.

Yet their bravery and loyalty saved countless lives.

In many ways, some of the most courageous participants of World War II walked on four legs.

snippet.title: Kim Jong-il’s 2011 State Funeral
snippet.description:
On December 17, 2011, North Korean state media announced the death of Kim Jong-il, who had led the country since 1994 following the death of Kim Il-sung.

According to official reports, he died of a heart attack while traveling by train. The announcement was broadcast on December 19, 2011. A national mourning period was declared shortly after.

The state funeral took place on December 28, 2011, in the capital city of Pyongyang. The funeral procession moved through the city under snowfall and was accompanied by senior party and military officials.

Public gatherings were organized across the country during the mourning period. Entertainment activities were suspended, and national flags were lowered to half-mast until December 29, 2011.

Following his death, his son, Kim Jong-un, was publicly presented as the country’s new leader. Shortly afterward, he assumed top positions within the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea, the military, and the state.

Kim Jong-il’s body was placed in state at the Kumsusan Memorial Palace in Pyongyang, where his father’s body had previously been preserved.

This video documents the publicly released footage from that period.

snippet.title: Could World War 3 Start With Iran?
snippet.description:
Could World War 3 really start with Iran?

With rising tensions in the Middle East, many people are asking whether a regional conflict involving Iran could spiral into a global war. Social media headlines often jump straight to “World War 3,” but how realistic is that scenario?

Iran plays a major strategic role in the Middle East. It has influence through regional allies and proxy groups, and its tensions with the United States and Israel have been ongoing for decades. Flashpoints include nuclear development concerns, military strikes, sanctions, cyber operations, and regional militia activity.

But here’s the key question: what turns a regional conflict into a world war?

Historically, a world war requires:

Multiple global superpowers directly fighting each other

Formal military alliances activating across continents

Sustained, large-scale warfare involving major economies

Right now, while tensions may escalate at times, most global powers are cautious. Even when strikes or retaliation occur, countries often aim to avoid full-scale escalation. Diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions, and backchannel negotiations are frequently used to prevent wider war.

Another major factor is deterrence. Modern warfare between large powers—especially nuclear-armed states—comes with catastrophic risks. Because of that, leaders are typically very careful about crossing certain red lines.

That doesn’t mean the situation is harmless. Regional wars can be devastating and destabilizing. They can affect oil markets, global trade, migration patterns, and security policies worldwide. But “World War 3” is a very specific threshold — and we are not there.

So could a conflict involving Iran contribute to a larger global war? In theory, yes — if major powers directly clash and alliances activate.
Is that happening right now? No.

The situation is tense, complex, and evolving — but a global world war requires far more than regional confrontation.

Understanding history helps us separate fear-driven headlines from realistic geopolitical risk.
